subject: Commerce
title: Business Ownership and Trade Bodies
outline: Limited liability companies: private and public
Share and loan capital; types of shares
Co-operative societies: types, features, merits and demerits
Trade associations, chambers of commerce and trade unions

modules.title: Limited Liability Companies
modules.html:
Meaning

A limited liability company is an incorporated association of persons registered under CAMA. It is a separate legal entity with perpetual succession, and members' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares.

Private vs Public Company

BasisPrivate (Ltd)Public (Plc)
Members1 – 50Minimum 2, no maximum
Transfer of sharesRestrictedFreely transferable
Invitation to publicNot allowedAllowed (prospectus)
AccountsFiled with CACPublished to the public
Start of businessOn certificate of incorporationAlso needs a certificate of trading

Formation Documents

  1. Memorandum of Association – external constitution: name, registered office, objects, liability clause, share capital, association/subscription clause.
  2. Articles of Association – internal rules: rights of shareholders, meetings, voting, directors, dividends.
  3. Statement of share capital and returns of allotment, list of directors and declaration of compliance.
  4. Prospectus – public invitation to subscribe for shares (public companies only).

Types of Shares

  • Ordinary (equity) shares – fluctuating dividend, voting rights, paid last.
  • Preference shares – fixed dividend, paid before ordinary; may be cumulative, non-cumulative, participating or redeemable.
  • Deferred/founders' shares – held by promoters, paid last.

Debentures are loan capital, not shares; holders are creditors who receive fixed interest whether or not profit is made.

examples.q: A company has 2,000,000 ordinary shares of ₦1 each and 500,000 10% preference shares of ₦1. Distributable profit is ₦350,000. Find the dividend per ordinary share.
examples.a: Preference dividend \(=10\%\times500{,}000=₦50{,}000\). Balance for ordinary shareholders \(=350{,}000-50{,}000=₦300{,}000\). Dividend per share \(=\dfrac{300{,}000}{2{,}000{,}000}=₦0.15\) (15 kobo), i.e. a 15% dividend.

examples.q: A firm has total assets of ₦24,000,000 and current liabilities of ₦4,500,000, earning a net profit of ₦3,900,000. Compute capital employed and the return on capital employed.
examples.a: \( \text{Capital Employed} = 24{,}000{,}000 - 4{,}500{,}000 = ₦19{,}500{,}000 \). \( \text{ROCE} = \dfrac{3{,}900{,}000}{19{,}500{,}000}\times100 = 20\% \), meaning every ₦100 of long-term funds earns ₦20 profit.

modules.title: Public Corporations and Co-operatives
modules.html:
Public Corporations (Statutory Corporations)

Business organisations set up by an Act of Parliament, owned and financed by government to provide essential services, e.g. NNPC Ltd, NPA, CBN, NTA, TCN.

Features
  • Created by law; owned by the state.
  • Managed by a board appointed by government.
  • Financed by government subvention, loans and internally generated revenue.
  • Service rather than profit motive; monopoly power common.
Problems
  1. Bureaucracy and slow decision-making
  2. Political interference
  3. Inefficiency, corruption and mismanagement
  4. Persistent losses requiring subsidies

Privatisation is the transfer of ownership from government to private individuals; commercialisation keeps ownership but requires the enterprise to run profitably. In Nigeria the process is handled by the BPE under the National Council on Privatisation.

Co-operative Societies

A voluntary association of persons who pool resources to promote their common economic interest, run on the principle of one member, one vote and distributing surplus as dividend on patronage.

TypePurpose
Consumer co-operativeBuys in bulk and sells cheaply to members
Producer co-operativeMembers produce and market jointly
Credit/thrift societySavings and cheap loans to members
Marketing co-operativeGrades and sells members' produce
Multi-purpose co-operativeCombines two or more of the above

examples.q: A consumer co-operative has a surplus of ₦900,000 to be shared as dividend on patronage. Total member purchases were ₦18,000,000 and Musa bought goods worth ₦450,000. What is his dividend?
examples.a: Rate \(=\dfrac{900{,}000}{18{,}000{,}000}=0.05\) i.e. 5 kobo per naira. Musa receives \(=5\%\times450{,}000=₦22{,}500\). Note that the surplus follows patronage, not capital contributed.

examples.q: Give two arguments for and two against privatising a loss-making public corporation.
examples.a: For: private management improves efficiency and accountability; sale proceeds and later company tax boost government revenue. Against: essential services may become unaffordable as private owners chase profit; retrenchment raises unemployment and ownership may concentrate in a few hands.

modules.title: Trade Associations and Business Bodies
modules.html:
Trade Association

An association of firms in the same line of business formed to protect and promote their common interest, e.g. MAN (Manufacturers Association of Nigeria), NACCIMA, Bankers' Committee, NARTO.

Functions
  • Represents members before government on policy and taxation.
  • Sets standards and codes of conduct.
  • Collects and circulates trade statistics.
  • Settles disputes among members and negotiates with trade unions.
  • Organises training, exhibitions and trade fairs.

Chambers of Commerce

Association of businessmen and firms in a locality (e.g. Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry). Functions: organise trade fairs, issue certificates of origin, arbitrate disputes, publish trade information and advise government on commercial policy.

Trade Unions

Associations of workers formed to improve wages and working conditions. Types: craft, industrial, general and white-collar unions. Weapons include collective bargaining, strike, work-to-rule, picketing and go-slow. Central labour bodies in Nigeria: NLC and TUC.

Co-operative vs Company – quick contrast

BasisCo-operativeCompany
VotingOne member, one voteOne share, one vote
SurplusDividend on patronageDividend on shareholding
MotiveService to membersProfit maximisation

examples.q: Why would a small manufacturer of shoes join MAN?
examples.a: To gain a collective voice on tariffs, forex and power policy; to obtain market and cost data; to access training and trade fairs; and to use the association's arbitration and lobbying strength which he could not command alone.

examples.q: State three differences between a trade association and a trade union.
examples.a: Membership: firms/employers vs workers. Objective: protecting business interests vs improving wages and conditions. Weapons: lobbying and lock-out vs strike and collective bargaining.

quiz.q: The maximum number of members in a private limited company is
quiz.solution: CAMA sets 50 as the ceiling for a private company, excluding employee shareholders.

quiz.q: The document that states the objects of a company is the
quiz.solution: The memorandum governs the company's relationship with the outside world, including its objects.

options: Invite the public to buy shares
quiz.solution: Only public companies issue a prospectus inviting subscription for shares or debentures.
Debentures are loan capital; holders receive fixed interest and rank before shareholders.
Their dividend is fixed and paid before ordinary dividends.

quiz.q: Capital employed is best expressed as
quiz.solution: It measures the long-term funds invested in the business.

options: The company continues despite death of members
quiz.solution: As a separate legal person, the company survives changes in membership.

quiz.q: A public corporation is established by
quiz.solution: Statutory corporations are created by enabling legislation.

quiz.q: The main motive of a public corporation is
quiz.solution: Public corporations exist primarily to render essential public services.

quiz.q: In a co-operative society, voting is based on
quiz.solution: Democratic control means each member has a single vote regardless of shares held.

quiz.q: Surplus in a consumer co-operative is shared as
quiz.solution: Members are rewarded in proportion to their purchases, not their capital.

quiz.q: Transfer of a government enterprise to private owners is called
quiz.solution: Privatisation changes ownership; commercialisation only changes the way it is run.

quiz.q: Which body issues certificates of origin to exporters in Nigeria?
quiz.solution: Chambers of commerce certify the origin of goods for export.

quiz.q: A union of workers in the same craft is a
quiz.solution: Craft unions organise workers with the same skill, e.g. electricians.

quiz.q: Ordinary shareholders are described as risk bearers because
options: They are paid last in liquidation
They lend money to the firm
quiz.solution: Their dividend is uncertain and they rank last on winding up.

quiz.q: A certificate of trading is required by
options: A public company before commencing business
quiz.solution: A public company needs both the certificate of incorporation and the certificate of trading.
